newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai govt vows economic boost, analysts skeptical.
newsitem.headline: Thai govt vows economic boost, analysts skeptical.

text.p: Thailand's new government on Wednesday detailed major policy initiatives to tackle the slowing national economy, but economic analysts said the proposals were vague.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who took office earlier this month, vowed in a speech to Parliamnent to uphold fiscal discipline, reduce spending, deregulate the financial sector and stimulate the slowing economy.
Chavalit's heads a six-party coalition government that replaced the administration of previous premier Banharn Silpa-archa. Banharn was accused of economic mismanagement.
Analysts said the government had identified key economic woes afflicting the nation but had left markets and investors hungry for details on strategies and implementation.

"Anyone can present policy like that. It's too vague. At least there should be more details to assure us that the policy will be implemented in the right direction," said Arporn Chewakriengkrai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"On fiscal discipline, for example, the government should have at least spelt out that it will not allow fiscal deficits instead of just saying it will uphold fiscal discipline," she said.
Arporn also said the government had failed to spell out its policies on the direction it wants interest rates to take and on the future of the baht and the system under which it is fixed daily.

The government pledged that it would curb the current account gap, which the central bank expects to rise up to 8.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, by boosting savings and foreign exchange earnings and reducing spending.

Thailand's exports, the country's growth engine during the past decade, recorded the slowest growth in years in 1996, growing just 0.9 percent in the first nine months against 20 percent during the same period last year.

The government also vowed to develop Thai money and capital markets to boost regional competitiveness, and to deregulate the financial sector, maintain price stability and revive the depressed property sector.
Thailand's stock market is now at a three-year low as many foreign investors have left to invest elsewhere in the region following a year of political uncertainty.

"The overall picture looked fine. The government seemed to address the problems we are facing. But it should give us some hints on its measures and action plans," said Somjai Phagaphasvivat, a professor at Thammsart University.
Somjai said Wednesday's announcement painted some contradictory pictures.
"The government needed to tell us how to curb the current account deficit while at the same time seeking to expand various capital-intensive infrastructure projects," he said.
